title: lectures-lecture4
text:
Imagine you run a coffee shop and someone tells you, “the new espresso machine makes better lattes.” You can’t just take their word for it — but you also can’t test every possible latte forever. You need a disciplined way to look at a limited amount of evidence and decide whether it’s convincing enough to change your mind about the world.
That, in one sentence, is what hypothesis testing is: a structured procedure for deciding whether the evidence you observed is surprising enough, under a specific “boring” explanation, to abandon that boring explanation.
The “boring” explanation has a name: the null hypothesis, usually written \(H_0\). It’s the default, skeptical, nothing-interesting-is-happening claim — “the new machine is no better than the old one.” The competing, more interesting claim is the alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\) (or \(H_A\)) — “the new machine really is better.”


Because we’re making a decision under uncertainty, there are two distinct ways things can go wrong:









\(H_0\) is actually true
\(H_0\) is actually false




We reject \(H_0\)
Type I error (false alarm)
Correct decision (a “hit”)


We fail to reject \(H_0\)
Correct decision
Type II error (a miss)




A Type I error is convicting an innocent person — crying wolf.
A Type II error is letting a guilty person go — missing a real effect.

There is an unavoidable tension here: if you make it harder to convict (to protect innocent people), you will also let more guilty people go free. You cannot drive both error rates to zero at once with a fixed amount of evidence. Every hypothesis test is, in some sense, a negotiation between these two risks.
We give the Type I error rate a special name and treat it as something we control in advance: the significance level, \(\alpha\). Setting \(\alpha = 0.05\) is a promise: “if the null hypothesis is really true, I’m only willing to falsely reject it 5% of the time, in the long run, across many hypothetical repetitions of this study.”
The p-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of seeing evidence at least as extreme as what we actually observed. A small p-value means “this would have been a weird thing to see if nothing interesting were going on” — which is evidence (not proof) against \(H_0\). The p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. It’s the probability of the data (or more extreme data), computed by assuming \(H_0\) is true. These sound similar but are logically very different quantities — mixing them up is one of the most common errors in applied statistics.

title: lectures-lecture4
section: How much can the data even tell you? — Fisher information
text:
How much can the data even tell you? — Fisher information
Before we can talk about good tests, it helps to have a sense of how much a dataset can possibly tell you about an unknown quantity. This is the intuitive role of Fisher information.
Think of it this way: suppose you’re trying to estimate some unknown parameter \(\theta\). As \(\theta\) changes, the probability of seeing your particular data changes too. Fisher information measures how sharply the probability of your data changes as you nudge \(\theta\) around its true value.
For example, imagine you’re tuning an old analog radio dial to find a station. Fisher information is like the sharpness of the signal peak: - If the station comes in crystal-clear at exactly one dial position and turns to static the instant you move the dial even slightly, the peak is very sharp. It’s easy to pin down the right setting precisely — this corresponds to high Fisher information. - If the station sounds almost equally decent across a wide range of dial positions, the peak is flat. You could be off by a lot and barely notice — this corresponds to low Fisher information.
A few consequences fall out of this picture almost for free, without needing formulas:

More data generally means more (sharper) information.
High Fisher information means your best possible estimate of \(\theta\) will be precise (a low-variance estimator is achievable). Low Fisher information means even your best estimator will be noisy. This relationship — more information caps how much uncertainty you’re stuck with — is formalized by a result called the Cramer–Rao bound.
Fisher information also drives how good a hypothesis test can be. A test is really just a decision built on top of an estimate. If the data barely distinguishes nearby values of \(\theta\) (low information), it will also barely distinguish \(H_0\) from a nearby \(H_1\), and no clever test design can fix that — it’s a property of the data-generating process itself, not of your method.

You don’t need the formula to use this intuition, but for completeness: Fisher information is formally defined as the expected curvature (technically, the negative expected second derivative) of the log-likelihood function around the true parameter value.

title: lectures-lecture4
text:
What makes a test “best”? — Power
If we fix how many false alarms we’re willing to tolerate (\(\alpha\)), the natural next question is: among all tests with that same false-alarm rate, which one is best at catching real effects when they exist?
The probability that a test correctly rejects \(H_0\) when \(H_1\) is actually true is called the test’s power. Power isn’t a single number — it typically depends on how far the truth is from \(H_0\). A test might have great power for detecting a huge effect but poor power for detecting a subtle one. This is usually visualized with a power curve: power on the vertical axis, “true distance from \(H_0\)” on the horizontal axis.

title: lectures-lecture4
text:
A metal-detector analogy
Think of power like a metal detector at the beach.

\(\alpha\) is how sensitive you’ve set the machine to beep on plain sand (false alarms you’ve agreed to tolerate).
Power is the probability it beeps when there really is a coin buried at some depth.
A shallow coin (a big, obvious effect) is easy to detect — power near 1.
A deeply buried coin (a tiny, subtle effect) is hard to detect — power might be low even with a good machine.
A bigger, more sensitive metal detector (more data, or less noisy measurements — i.e., higher Fisher information) raises the whole power curve.


Uniformly Most Powerful (UMP) tests
A test is called Uniformly Most Powerful (UMP) at level \(\alpha\) if it has the highest possible power against every single alternative value of \(\theta\) simultaneously, among all tests with that same \(\alpha\).
The word “uniformly” is doing real work here — it means “no matter which specific alternative you check against, this test wins (or ties).” That’s a very strong requirement:
A UMP test is is a remarkable, somewhat rare situation. It tends to happen only in “nice,” simple settings. A good example is when when you’re comparing one specific value of \(\theta\) against alternatives that all sit on one side of it (a one-sided test, e.g., \(H_0: \theta \le \theta_0\) vs. \(H_1: \theta > \theta_0\)), in models with a well-behaved structure (a monotone likelihood ratio).
When alternatives sit on both sides (a two-sided test, \(H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0\)), a single test almost never dominates every alternative in both directions at once. UMP tests generally fail to exist in the two-sided case, which is why two-sided testing usually settles for a good, sensible compromise test rather than a provably-best one.

title: lectures-lecture4
text:
The Neyman–Pearson Lemma (heuristically)
So how do you actually build a most-powerful test, at least when comparing one simple hypothesis to another? This is exactly what the Neyman–Pearson Lemma answers.
Suppose you must choose between exactly two fully specified possibilities: \(H_0: \theta = \theta_0\) versus \(H_1: \theta = \theta_1\). For any dataset you might observe, you can ask: “how much more likely is this data under \(H_1\) than under \(H_0\)?” That ratio is called the likelihood ratio.
The Neyman–Pearson lemma says: the best possible test is the one that rejects \(H_0\) exactly when the evidence favors \(H_1\) over \(H_0\) by more than some cutoff — i.e., rank every possible dataset by “how much more \(H_1\)-like than \(H_0\)-like is it,” and reject \(H_0\) for the most extreme, most \(H_1\)-favoring outcomes, until you’ve used up your allotted false-alarm budget \(\alpha\).
Why is this optimal, intuitively? Because you’re spending your fixed “false alarm budget” (\(\alpha\)) exactly where it buys the most power — on the outcomes that are most diagnostic of \(H_1\) over \(H_0\). Any other rule for deciding when to reject would, for the same \(\alpha\), end up flagging some outcomes that are less diagnostic while ignoring others that are more diagnostic — leaving power on the table. It’s the statistical version of “spend your limited budget on the highest-value evidence first.”
This simple-versus-simple result is also the conceptual seed of UMP tests: when a UMP test does exist (as in the one-sided, well-behaved cases described above), it’s usually because the likelihood-ratio test from the Neyman–Pearson lemma turns out to be the same test, no matter which specific alternative \(\theta_1\) you plug in — so the one test that’s best against one alternative happens to be best against all of them simultaneously.

title: lectures-lecture4
text:
Putting it all together
The throughline connecting all of this is worth stating plainly:

Fisher information tells you the fundamental ceiling on how precisely your data can pin down an unknown parameter — the sharpness of the radio dial’s peak.
Power tells you how good a specific test is at detecting real effects, given that ceiling — how good your metal detector is at any given burial depth.
UMP tests are the (rare, special-case) tests that are simultaneously the best metal detector at every possible depth.
The Neyman–Pearson lemma tells you exactly how to build the best possible test when comparing two fully specified hypotheses — rank evidence by how much more it favors \(H_1\) over \(H_0\), and reject in the most favoring cases — and this same likelihood-ratio logic is the reason UMP tests exist at all in the one-sided cases where they do.

title: 8/31 Lecture 2
text:
Today we’re going to explore a few cases where real statistics were computed effectively and correctly on paper, yet completely failed their purpose. Statistics, as with most other things, depends heavily on interpretation – when the interpretation fails, our research is no longer sound.
Correlation vs. Causation
Let’s think about a classic example. Ice cream sales and the number of shark attacks both increase in the summer. Does this mean that eating ice cream causes more people to get chased by sharks? Obviously, this is not what’s going on here – the season itself is causing both of these events independently (more humans in the ocean in the summer = more shark injuries. hotter weather = a greater need for ice cream). Even though ice cream sales and shark attacks are correlated (move together), one does not necessarily cause the other.
Keep this in mind as you dissect any research paper in the following weeks, and you’ll easily find reason for skepticism everywhere.
Confounding Variables
In the case of the ice cream sales and shark attacks, there was a hidden, confounding third variable that influenced both variables of interest, making them seem related. As we explore these papers, think about what differs between the two groups examined, or other variables that might be at play.
Sample Size and Generalizability
Before we trust any findings, and thinking back to our discussion last week, it’s important to consider the sample size of the study. How many people did the survey ask? Which groups of people was this pattern found in? The original marshmallow study we’re about to read was conducted on a small sample of children at a preschool on Stanford’s campus. As you read, consider what impact this may have on the results.
Replication
Replication is basically redoing a study, ideally with a bigger, more representative sample. The goal of this is to see if the original result appears once again, to help validate or question the original study’s results. One of today’s readings is a replication attempt of the marshmallow test. Note what differs between replication attempts, not limited to the results! Did the replication increase sample size, or change the population experimented on? How might that impact our interpretations of both studies’ findings?

title: 8/31 Lecture 2
text:
Non-Experimental / Observational Studies
In observational studies, the investigator does not control who is exposed to a risk factor or intervention. Instead, exposures occur naturally, and the researcher measures associations between exposure and outcome. These studies are further divided by their unit of analysis: population-based or individual-based.

Population-Based Studies
These studies use aggregate, group-level data rather than data on individual subjects.

Descriptive — Health Survey

Health Survey

Describes the distribution of health-related states or events in a population, typically in terms of person, place, and time (the “who, where, and when”). It does not test hypotheses about cause and effect — it simply characterizes the burden of disease or health status in a defined population at a point in time.




Analytic — Ecological Study

Ecological Study

Compares exposure and outcome data across groups or populations (e.g., countries, cities, or regions) rather than individuals. It looks for correlations between an exposure rate and a disease rate at the population level. While useful for generating hypotheses, ecological studies are vulnerable to the ecological fallacy — the risk of wrongly inferring individual-level relationships from group-level data.





Individual-Based Studies
These studies collect and analyze data on individual subjects rather than groups.

Descriptive — Case Reports and Case Series

Case Report

A detailed description of a single, often unusual or novel, clinical case. Case Series


Describes a group of patients with a similar diagnosis or exposure, without a comparison group.


Both are hypothesis-generating tools that document clinical observations but cannot establish causal relationships due to the absence of a control group.


Analytic Studies - hi
Analytic studies test specific hypotheses about the relationship between an exposure and an outcome, typically using a comparison group. There are three main designs:

Cross-Sectional Study (Prevalence Study)

Measures exposure and outcome simultaneously in a population at a single point in time. It estimates the prevalence of disease and can identify associations, but because exposure and outcome are measured at the same time, it cannot establish the temporal sequence needed to infer causation.

Case-Control Study (Case-Reference Study)

Starts with subjects who already have the outcome of interest (cases) and compares them to those without it (controls), looking backward to assess prior exposure. This design is efficient for studying rare diseases and is retrospective in nature.

Cohort Study (Follow-Up Study)

Begins with a group of exposed and unexposed individuals who are free of the outcome, then follows them forward in time to compare the incidence of disease between groups. Cohort studies can be prospective or retrospective and provide stronger evidence of temporal sequence than cross-sectional or case-control designs.

title: 8/31 Lecture 2
text:
Experimental / Interventional Studies
In experimental studies, the investigator actively assigns the exposure or intervention, allowing for stronger causal inference than observational designs.

Randomized Control Trial (Clinical Trial)
Participants are randomly assigned to receive either the intervention (e.g., a drug or treatment) or a control/placebo. Randomization balances known and unknown confounding factors between groups, making the RCT the gold standard for establishing causality. When conducted in a clinical setting, this is often called a clinical trial.


Non-Randomized (Quasi-Experimental) Studies
When randomization is not feasible or ethical, researchers may use non-randomized designs:

Quasi-Experimental Study: An intervention is assigned without random allocation, often using pre-existing groups (e.g., comparing outcomes before and after a policy change).
Field Trial: The intervention is applied to healthy individuals in the community (rather than a clinical setting) who are at risk of developing a disease, often to test preventive measures like vaccines.
Community Trial: The unit of intervention and analysis is an entire community or group, rather than individuals — commonly used to evaluate public health interventions such as water fluoridation or health education campaigns.

Let’s consider a world where statistics doesn’t exist. What would it look like? People could make random claims without numerical evidence. Your feed would look like a random mess of videos constantly being posted. One could argue that we couldn’t count the number of people enrolled in this course.
Okay, well that seemed pretty obvious. Of course, the reason for taking this course is likely some form of personal interest, as it’s a random half credit house course. Perhaps you’re a CS major who wants to learn some statistical algorithms to recreate Google’s PageRank. Maybe you’re a pre-med and hope to do a survival analysis to support your research interests. Finally, maybe you’re a sociologist and want to determine a population parameter for the use of AI in the classroom.
Let’s reflect on what today’s world looks like. A reasonable statement would be: “Statistics exists. We also hope that you’ll be able to critically evaluate the quality of a statistical analysis on a paper you’ve never seen before. There is much to learn!

title: 8/24 Lecture 1
section: What is statistics? What is a statistic?
text:
What is statistics? What is a statistic?
Statistics (the field) is a mathematical science pertaining to the collection, analysis, interpretation, and presentation of data.
A statistic is any quantity computed from values in a sample. That is incredibly broad. During this course, we will primarily focus on two types of statistics (which are not mutually exclusive of one another):


Descriptive statistics, which summarize a sample of data


Test statistics, which is some number derived from the sample that would be selected or defined in a way that differentiates between the null and alternative hypothesis.

That’s a lot of jargon right there. No worries – we’ll break it down through this course!

title: 8/24 Lecture 1
text:
“Good” statistics vs. “Bad” statistics
What is “good” statistics? In this case, we typically will mean rigorous, with clearly defined intentions, acknowledgement of shortcomings, and evaluation of its efficacy in practice. This would make a “good” statistic (singular) one that is appropriate to use in the given scenario.
A short example. Say you’ve got a bunch of categorical data (ex: survey answers of Yes or No), but then you create some model that only models continuous data (ex: representing Yes as 1 and No as 0, and having statistics in between). That’s not good! You may even get a statistically significant result (we will learn what this really means). Say you even made it past the editors at a publishing house and got published, and some random news reporter picked it up and wrote an article on it. We will see later in this course that this has actually happened many, many times.
In this course, we will read some very good and very bad papers. Ideally, you’ll be able to determine why they’re bad, beyond simply “the journal retracted them.”
What good statistics should do

Make data more approachable. A statistic should be well-chosen summary that allows the audience to understand something about, for example, the opinions of 10,000 people without having to look at all 10,000 data points.
Support a claim. Statistics should typically have a goal/purpose that they are attempting to explain, or identify some specific finding.
Display relevant information. The statistic chosen should actually speak to the question being asked!
Communicate a story. At the end of the day, someone has to be able to view your analysis and understand what it conveys and its implications.

What bad statistics may do

Use methods inappropriately. For example, applying a statistical technique to data it wasn’t designed for. We’ll explore lots of papers that do this!
Adding unnecessary complexity. Sometimes, complexity can obscure the true result. Often times, simple is best.
Cherry-picking or overgeneralizing. Selectively reporting the data points (or the one significant test out of twenty) that support your narrative, or taking a result from a small, biased, or narrow sample and claiming it holds for the larger group.

Why do we care?
You all have probably seen your fair share of misleading or crazy news headlines. From Scientists Say Smelling Farts Might Prevent Cancer to Coffee Consumption May Raise Miscarriage Risk, our world is full of bad statistics. Language like “might” or “may” largely obscure the actual scientific findings of correlation vs. causation.
And beyond clickbait news articles and AI Instagram posts, bad statistics also show up in legitimate, peer-reviewed research. Consider a study on physician age at death by specialty: emergency physicians were reported to have the youngest average age at death (58.7 years!) of any medical specialty. But this estimate was based on only 43 obituaries (compared to primary care physicians, whose average statistic was based on 2,508). A mean built on 43 observations is going to be far noisier than one built on thousands, even though both are presented in the same table, in the same font, with the same weight. This is just one example of the importance of statistical literacy and thinking critically about research.

title: 8/24 Lecture 1
text:
Research 101
Turning now to the second half of our course title, research – where does statistics play a role? How does the research process work?

Understand the field: Research usually starts with lots and lots of reading. We want to be able to know what’s already been asked and what answers already exist before we can possibly understand what’s missing.
Find a new question: A good question is specific, testable, and not already answered! This is where research truly starts.
Find a way to test the question: We usually want to design a study or analysis that could actually provide evidence for or against your question.
Examine/analyze the results: Running said test, computing the numbers, reporting findings.
and finally, write about it and why it matters.

Step 4 is where most think statistics starts and ends.
But really, it’s active all the way back in Step 2, before any data has been manipulated. When we are finding our question, we need to define our variables, or subject(s) of interest. What exactly are we measuring? How are we measuring them? Vague variables lead to vague (or unanswerable) questions!
In Step 3, when we’re designing a study or analysis to test our question, that design may play a significant impact on the strength of the answer we will get. For example, our question may be about a causal relationship (does X cause Y?), but our study design may only be able to give us a correlational answer (X and Y are/are not related).
It’s also tempting to think that statistics ends when we’ve done the analysis, and all that’s left is to write it out in nice sentences. But Step 5 is arguably the most important part. Communication of statistics is extremely important. Vocabulary such as “significant” means something very specific in a statistical context compared to colloquial usage. Additionally, we must make the conclusion as clear as possible to our audience, or else we might end up with a headline as striking as farts preventing cancer.

title: 8/24 Lecture 1
section: Keshav, S. “How to Read a Paper”
text:
Keshav, S. “How to Read a Paper”
Before diving headfirst into research papers (as we will in the rest of this course), it’s important to know how to read one efficiently and effectively, especially if we don’t know much about the topic. “Researchers spend a great deal reading research papers. However this skill is rarely taught, leading to much wasted effort,” Keshav introduces. How to Read a Paper proposes a three-pass method for reading academic research papers:

The first pass: a quick skim of the title, abstract, introduction, section headings, and conclusions. The goal is to get a general gist of what the paper does, how it does it, and whether it’s worth diving into.
The second pass: a more careful read, now looking into figures, diagrams, data, etc., but still not exploring too much detail. The goal is to understand the general content and be able to summarize it with some supporting evidence.
The third pass: a full read, where the goal is to “virtually re-implement” the paper, or be able to reconstruct its structure and challenge its assumptions, methods, and results.

Class Discussion Questions:

What was your previous method of reading papers? How has this changed your perspective?

Are there any helpful tips/tricks you’ve developed/found on your own when reading articles or papers?

Why does this method matter? Why should we deeply learn and understand a paper?
Why is point 3 (“Doing a Literature Survey”) important in research?
How do you think point 4 (“Experience”) develops?

Use of outside resources, including AI
There are at least two reasons you might seek outside resources:

Extra practice/material or alternative instruction: Go crazy. Knock yourself out. Have a ball. The internet is saturated with good (and horrible) resources for learning this material, so if you find something that really resonates with you, have at it;
Doing the work for you: If you ask a language model to generate a summary, and you copy it down and submit it as your own work, that is plagiarism. If we detect it, you will earn a zero for that part of your write-up.

“Using ChatGPT to complete assignments is like bringing a forklift into the weight room; you will never improve your cognitive fitness that way.” Furthermore, this course is a half-credit, pass-fail course purely for your own interest. As such, outsourcing all of your thinking to an AI will probably end in this entire enterprise being a complete waste of time and energy. To avoid this, we suggest you abstain from using language models to do the reading/thinking for you.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
text:
Before we can talk about hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, p-values, or any of the machinery of statistical inference, we need a shared vocabulary for describing uncertainty. Every measurement you will ever collect in research — a survey response, a lab reading, a reaction time, a clinical outcome — is, in some sense, the result of a random process. Probability is simply the mathematical language we use to describe how likely different outcomes of that random process are.
A probability distribution is just a complete description of “what can happen” and “how likely each thing is to happen.” Everything in this chapter is really just different flavors of that one idea, applied to different kinds of research questions.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
text:
Random Variables: Naming the Outcome
A random variable is nothing more than a name we give to the outcome of some process we haven’t observed yet, or whose outcome varies from instance to instance.

Flip a coin: let \(X = 1\) if heads, 0 if tails.
Count the number of patients who respond to a treatment out of 50 enrolled: let \(X\) = that count.
Measure a participant’s reaction time in milliseconds: let \(X\) = that time.

Notice the first two examples can only take specific, countable values (0, 1, 2, 3, …). We call these discrete random variables. The third example, reaction time, could in principle take any value on a continuum (300.2 ms, 300.21 ms, 300.213 ms, …). We call these continuous random variables.
This distinction matters because it changes how we talk about probability:

For a discrete variable, we can ask directly: “what is the probability \(X\) equals exactly 3?”
For a continuous variable, asking for the probability of one exact value (like “reaction time equals exactly 300.213000… ms”) doesn’t really make sense — there are infinitely many possible values, so any single one has essentially zero probability. Instead, we ask about ranges: “what’s the probability the reaction time is between 290 and 310 ms?”

Binomial, geometric, negative binomial, and Poisson are all discrete. Normal is continuous.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
text:
Counting First: How “Choose” Works
Several distributions below need us to count the number of ways something can happen, not just whether it happens. The classic example: if you flip a coin 4 times and want exactly 2 heads, there’s more than one way to arrange that — HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH. Six arrangements, all equally consistent with “2 heads out of 4 flips.”
This is where the choose operation comes in, written \(\binom{n}{k}\) and read “n choose k.” It answers exactly one question:
“Out of \(n\) total slots, in how many distinct ways can you pick \(k\) of them to be”successes” (without caring about the order you picked them in)?”
You don’t need to memorize the formula to use the intuition, but here it is for reference:
\[\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\]
where \(n! = n \times (n-1) \times (n-2) \times \cdots \times 1\) (“n factorial”) counts the number of ways to fully order \(n\) items.
Think of \(\binom{n}{k}\) as answering: “how many different-looking outcomes give me the same total count of successes?” This is exactly the gap between “the probability of one specific sequence” and “the probability of a certain number of successes, in any order.” The choose function bridges that gap by counting the arrangements. It shows up explicitly in the binomial and negative binomial distributions below, and implicitly everywhere we count “how many ways.”
You will almost never compute \(\binom{n}{k}\) by hand in this course — software does it instantly (choose(n, k) in R, math.comb(n, k) in Python). What matters is recognizing when a problem is a counting problem in disguise.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
section: Mean and Variance: Two Numbers That Summarize a Distribution
text:
Mean and Variance: Two Numbers That Summarize a Distribution
Before walking through specific distributions, it helps to fix ideas about the two numbers we’ll report for each one.

The mean (also called the expected value, written \(E[X]\)) is the long-run average outcome if you could repeat the random process infinitely many times. It is a measure of central tendency — where the distribution is “centered.”
The variance (written \(\text{Var}(X)\)) measures how spread out the outcomes tend to be around that mean. A small variance means outcomes cluster tightly around the mean; a large variance means they’re scattered widely. The standard deviation is just the square root of the variance, and is often more interpretable because it’s back in the original units of \(X\) rather than squared units.

If mean is “where’s the center of the dartboard,” variance is “how tightly clustered are the darts around that center.” Two archers can have the exact same average hit location and wildly different consistency.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
text:
Discrete Distributions
All of the discrete distributions below are built out of the same atomic idea: a Bernoulli trial — a single yes/no, success/failure event with some fixed probability \(p\) of success. Think: one coin flip, one patient responding to treatment, one email being spam. Everything else in this section is a story about “repeating” or “waiting for” Bernoulli trials.

The Binomial Distribution: “How many successes in a fixed number of tries?”
Say you run a fixed number of independent trials, \(n\), each with the same probability of success \(p\). You count the total number of successes, \(X\). That’s binomial. For example, out of 30 patients on a treatment, how many recover within a week?
Why “choose” shows up: To get exactly \(k\) successes out of \(n\) trials, you need (a) the probability of any one specific arrangement of \(k\) successes and \(n-k\) failures, which is \(p^k (1-p)^{n-k}\), times (b) the number of arrangements that produce that same count, which is \(\binom{n}{k}\). Multiply those together and you get the binomial probability formula:
\[P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}\]
Mean and variance:
\[E[X] = np \qquad \text{Var}(X) = np(1-p)\]
Intuition: if each of \(n\) trials has probability \(p\) of success, the average total is simply \(n\) times \(p\) — you’d expect 30% of 100 trials to succeed if \(p = 0.3\). The variance is largest when \(p = 0.5\) (maximum uncertainty about each individual trial) and shrinks as \(p\) moves toward 0 or 1 (each trial becomes more predictable).


The Geometric Distribution: “How long until the first success?”
Instead of fixing the number of trials and counting successes, we now fix the goal (get one success) and count how many Bernoulli trials it takes to get there. For example, how many samples must a lab process before finding the first contaminated one?
Mean and variance:
\[E[X] = \frac{1}{p} \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \frac{1-p}{p^2}\]
Intuition: if success happens with probability \(p\) on each trial, you’d expect to wait about \(1/p\) trials for it to show up — a rare event (\(p\) small) takes a long average wait, a common event (\(p\) close to 1) resolves almost immediately. Note that unlike the binomial, there’s no upper limit to how many trials you might need — in principle you could wait forever, which is part of why the variance formula looks different.


The Negative Binomial Distribution: “How long until the r-th success?”
This is the natural generalization of the geometric distribution. Instead of waiting for the first success, we wait for the \(r\)-th success, for any fixed number \(r\).For example, how many patients must be screened before you’ve enrolled 20 eligible participants?
Just like the binomial needed a “choose” term to count arrangements, the negative binomial needs one too — because the \(r\)-th success can be preceded by its \(r-1\) earlier successes landing in any order among the trials that came before it.
Mean and variance:
\[E[X] = \frac{r}{p} \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}\]
Intuition: this is exactly \(r\) copies of the geometric distribution’s logic stacked together — if it takes \(1/p\) trials on average to get one success, it takes roughly \(r\) times that to get \(r\) of them. Set \(r = 1\) and these formulas collapse exactly to the geometric distribution’s formulas above — a good sanity check that the two distributions are genuinely nested inside one another.
In practice, the negative binomial distribution is also widely used to model overdispersed count data — count data (like the Poisson, below) but with more variability than a Poisson distribution allows. You’ll see this especially in count-based outcome models (e.g., number of hospital visits, number of citations) where a plain Poisson model underestimates the true spread of the data.


The Poisson Distribution: “How many events occur in a fixed window?”
The Poisson distribution answers a different kind of question than the previous three. Instead of counting successes out of a known number of discrete trials, it counts the number of times a rare event happens over a continuous window of time, space, or exposure — where events could, in principle, happen at any moment, but tend to happen at some known average rate, denoted \(\lambda\) (“lambda”). For example, the number of customer complaints a call center receives per hour. - Number of mutations observed per strand of DNA of a fixed length. - Number of earthquakes in a region per year.
Why it’s different from the binomial: notice there’s no natural “\(n\)” here — no fixed number of trials. There’s no ceiling on how many complaints a call center could receive in an hour. The Poisson distribution is actually what the binomial distribution turns into if you imagine \(n\) (the number of “chances” for an event) growing towards infinity while \(p\) (the chance of an event on any one of them) shrinks towards zero, in just the right balance that the average number of events, \(np\), settles on a fixed value \(\lambda\). This is a useful bridge to keep in mind: Poisson is the limit of binomial when trials become so frequent and individually so unlikely that all that matters is the overall rate.
Mean and variance:
\[E[X] = \lambda \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \lambda\]
Intuition: this is the single most distinctive feature of the Poisson distribution — the mean and variance are the same number. If a process averages 4 events per hour, its variance is also 4 (and so its standard deviation is 2, the square root of 4). This is a strong, testable assumption: real-world count data that is more variable than its own mean (“overdispersed”) is a signal that a plain Poisson model is too simple — which is exactly the situation where researchers often reach for the negative binomial instead.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
section: The Continuous Case: The Normal Distribution
text:
The Continuous Case: The Normal Distribution
Every distribution so far counted something discrete. The normal distribution (also called the Gaussian, or “bell curve”) is the workhorse continuous distribution in research, used to model quantities that can vary smoothly: height, blood pressure, measurement error, standardized test scores, and — critically for later in this course — the sampling distributions of many statistics themselves (a preview of the Central Limit Theorem, which you’ll meet properly in the hypothesis testing unit).
The shape: symmetric, bell-shaped, single peak at the mean, tapering smoothly off to either side. It is described completely by just two numbers:
\[E[X] = \mu \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2\]
where \(\mu\) (“mu”) is the mean — the center and peak of the bell — and \(\sigma^2\) (“sigma squared”) is the variance, controlling how wide or narrow the bell is. A small \(\sigma^2\) produces a tall, narrow bell (values tightly clustered near \(\mu\)); a large \(\sigma^2\) produces a short, wide bell (values spread out).

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
text:
The 68–95–99.7 rule
A useful heuristic you’ll use constantly: for a normal distribution, roughly 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% fall within 2 standard deviations, and 99.7% fall within 3 standard deviations. This single rule of thumb will get you very far in reasoning about normal data without ever touching the underlying formula.
Unlike the discrete distributions above, there’s no clean “story” of counting or waiting behind the normal distribution’s formula, and we won’t write that formula out here — for this course, what matters is the shape, the two parameters that control it, and the 68–95–99.7 rule for reasoning about spread. The formula becomes important later; the intuition is what carries you through most applied statistical reasoning.

title: 9/7 Lecture 3
section: Bayes’ Rule: Updating Beliefs With Evidence
text:
Bayes’ Rule: Updating Beliefs With Evidence
Everything so far described the probability of outcomes before we observe any data. But research is fundamentally about updating what we believe once evidence comes in. Bayes’ rule is the formal recipe for doing that update correctly.

The Intuition First
Suppose you’re testing patients for a rare disease. A patient tests positive. What’s the probability they actually have the disease?
Your instinct might be “well, the test is 99% accurate, so 99%.” But this ignores something crucial: how rare the disease is in the first place. If the disease is extremely rare, most positive tests will actually be false positives from the huge pool of healthy people, not true positives from the tiny pool of sick people. Bayes’ rule is the formal machinery for combining how rare the disease is (your belief before the test — the prior) with how reliable the test is (the new evidence) to get the correct updated belief (the posterior).
Bayes’ rule says: your updated belief about something should combine (1) how likely you thought it was before seeing the evidence, and (2) how surprising the evidence would be under each possible explanation. Evidence that would be very surprising if a hypothesis were false is strong evidence in favor of that hypothesis — but only relative to how believable the hypothesis was to begin with.


The Formula
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\, P(A)}{P(B)}\]
Read the pieces one at a time:

\(P(A)\) — the prior: how likely \(A\) (e.g., “has the disease”) was before any evidence.
\(P(B \mid A)\) — the likelihood: how likely the evidence \(B\) (e.g., “tested positive”) is, assuming \(A\) is true.
\(P(B)\) — the overall probability of seeing the evidence \(B\) at all, across every possible explanation (sick or healthy).
\(P(A \mid B)\) — the posterior: your updated belief about \(A\), now that you’ve seen \(B\).

The notation \(P(A \mid B)\) is read “the probability of \(A\) given \(B\)” — it’s how we write “conditional on already knowing \(B\) happened, how likely is \(A\)?” This is the central idea behind everything Bayes’ rule does: it converts between \(P(B \mid A)\) (which is often what we can measure directly, like test accuracy) and \(P(A \mid B)\) (which is usually what we actually want to know, like “does this patient have the disease?”). These two conditional probabilities are not the same thing, and confusing them is one of the most common reasoning errors in applied research — Bayes’ rule exists precisely to keep them straight.
Bayes’ rule underlies an entire branch of statistical inference (Bayesian statistics), but even researchers working in the more traditional (“frequentist”) framework rely on this logic constantly — anytime you interpret a diagnostic test, a screening tool, or evidence of any kind, you are implicitly reasoning about priors, likelihoods, and posteriors, whether or not you write the formula down.

Today’s lecture is about applying that machinery to one of the most common jobs in applied statistics: comparing groups. Is Drug A better than Drug B? Do three different teaching methods produce different test scores? Is a coin-flip outcome associated with which treatment a patient received?
The punchline to keep in your back pocket: every test in this lecture is still just a hypothesis test, in the exact sense of Lecture 4 — a null hypothesis, a test statistic, a null distribution, a p-value. What changes from test to test is only: what kind of outcome data you have, and what structural assumptions you’re willing to make. Once you see that, the whole zoo of named tests stops looking like a pile of unrelated recipes and starts looking like one recipe with a few swappable ingredients.
Before picking a test, ask: “is my outcome variable continuous (like a measurement) or categorical (like a label)?” This single fork explains most of the test names you’ll see below. A secondary question — “how many groups am I comparing, and are the groups independent or matched/paired?” — determines the rest.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: Comparing two groups on a continuous outcome
text:
Comparing two groups on a continuous outcome

The independent-samples t-test
Setting: You have a continuous outcome (heights, test scores, reaction times) measured on two separate, unrelated groups — e.g., a treatment group and a control group, where each subject belongs to only one group.

title: lectures-lecture5
text:
The intuition: signal versus noise
The t-test is built on one core idea: is the difference between the two group averages large relative to how much the data naturally jitters around within each group?
Imagine comparing the average height of two basketball teams. If every player on Team A is close to 6’8” and every player on Team B is close to 6’2”, a small sample is enough to convince you the teams really differ — the “noise” (within-group spread) is small relative to the “signal” (between-group gap). But if heights within each team already range wildly from 5’10” to 7’0”, the same 6-inch gap between team averages is much less convincing — it could easily be due to who happened to get measured.
This ratio-of-signal-to-noise idea is captured, with only a little math, by the t-statistic:
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\text{standard error of that difference}}\]
The numerator is the signal (how far apart the group averages are); the denominator is essentially the noise, scaled by how much data you have. A t-statistic far from zero means the signal comfortably outpaces the noise.

title: lectures-lecture5
text:
What the t-test assumes

Independence: each observation doesn’t influence any other (no repeated measurements on the same subject across groups).
Approximate normality of the outcome within each group (or a large enough sample size that the Central Limit Theorem bails you out).
Equal variances across the two groups, in the classic (“Student’s”) version. In practice, most software now defaults to Welch’s t-test, a small modification that doesn’t require equal variances — a strictly safer default with almost no downside, so there’s rarely a reason not to use it.


The paired t-test
Setting: The same continuous outcome, but now the two measurements are linked — before/after measurements on the same subjects, or matched pairs (twins, matched patients).

title: lectures-lecture5
section: The intuition: cancel out what you can’t control for
text:
The intuition: cancel out what you can’t control for
If you measure the same 20 people’s blood pressure before and after a new medication, each person is their own built-in control — a naturally high-blood-pressure person will likely still be somewhat high after treatment, regardless of whether the drug worked. The paired t-test exploits this by working with the 20 within-person differences rather than the raw before/after numbers, which cancels out person-to-person variability that has nothing to do with the treatment.
This is why pairing (when available) is so powerful: it strips out a whole source of noise before the comparison even starts, which — recalling Lecture 1’s Fisher information idea — effectively sharpens the “signal peak” the test has to work with.
Mechanically, a paired t-test is just a one-sample t-test performed on the differences, testing whether the average difference is zero.

Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test)
Setting: Same two-independent-groups situation as the independent t-test — but you’re worried the normality assumption is badly violated (e.g., strongly skewed data, obvious outliers, or an outcome that’s only ordinal — ranked categories like “mild / moderate / severe” rather than a true continuous measurement).

title: lectures-lecture5
section: The intuition: forget the exact numbers, just look at the ranking
text:
The intuition: forget the exact numbers, just look at the ranking
Instead of comparing averages, the Mann-Whitney U test throws all the data (both groups combined) into one pile, ranks every observation from smallest to largest, and then asks: “if I hadn’t looked at group labels, would the ranks from Group A tend to be systematically higher or lower than the ranks from Group B?”
Concretely: pick one random observation from Group A and one from Group B — what’s the probability the one from Group A is larger? Under \(H_0\) (no difference), that probability should be exactly 50/50, like a fair coin flip. The Mann-Whitney U statistic essentially counts, across every possible A-vs-B pairing, how often A “wins,” and checks whether that win rate is suspiciously far from 50%.
Because this test only uses the ordering of the data, not the exact numeric gaps, it’s far less sensitive to outliers or skewed distributions than the t-test — you’re trading a little bit of statistical power (when the t-test’s assumptions genuinely hold) for a lot of robustness (when they don’t). It also formally tests a slightly different, more general hypothesis than the t-test — roughly “are the two distributions shifted relative to one another?” rather than specifically “do the two means differ?” — which is part of why it works even for ordinal (ranked) rather than truly numeric data.

Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The nonparametric counterpart to the paired t-test: instead of averaging the raw within-pair differences, it ranks the absolute sizes of the differences, re-attaches the original + / − signs, and asks whether the positive-ranked and negative-ranked differences are roughly balanced (as they should be under \(H_0\): no systematic before/after change) or lopsided.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: Comparing three or more groups on a continuous outcome
text:
Comparing three or more groups on a continuous outcome

One-way ANOVA (Analysis of Variance)
Setting: A continuous outcome, three or more independent groups — e.g., comparing test scores across three different teaching methods.
You might reasonably ask: “why not just run a t-test on every pair of groups?” The answer is one of the most important intuitions in this lecture.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: Why not just run lots of t-tests? The multiple-comparisons problem
text:
Why not just run lots of t-tests? The multiple-comparisons problem
Every individual t-test carries some false-alarm risk (\(\alpha\), say 5%). If you compare 3 groups pairwise, that’s 3 separate tests; with 10 groups, it’s 45 tests. Even if no real differences exist anywhere, running enough separate 5%-risk tests makes it increasingly likely that at least one of them will show “significance” purely by chance — like rolling enough dice that someone eventually rolls a run of sixes.
ANOVA solves this by asking one single, combined question first — “is there evidence that any of the group means differ, considered all at once?” — controlling the overall false-alarm rate at your chosen \(\alpha\) for that one big question, rather than letting it balloon across many small ones.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: The intuition: comparing two kinds of “spread”
text:
The intuition: comparing two kinds of “spread”
ANOVA’s core trick is right there in the name: it works by comparing two different ways of measuring variance in the data.

Between-group variance: how much do the group averages differ from the overall grand average? (If the teaching methods really matter, group averages should scatter widely around the overall mean.)
Within-group variance: how much do individual data points differ from their own group’s average? (This is just natural noise/spread that exists no matter what.)

If the groups are truly different, the between-group variance should be large relative to the within-group variance — the group averages should stand out clearly above the background noise. If the groups don’t really differ, both kinds of variance should be roughly comparable, because any apparent differences between group averages are just what you’d expect from random noise alone.
This ratio is the F-statistic:
\[F = \frac{\text{between-group variance}}{\text{within-group variance}}\]
An F-statistic much larger than 1 says “the groups are more spread out from each other than random noise alone would explain” — evidence against \(H_0\) (all group means equal).

title: lectures-lecture5
section: ANOVA only tells you that something differs, not what
text:
ANOVA only tells you that something differs, not what
A significant ANOVA result means “not all group means are equal” — full stop. It doesn’t say which group(s) differ from which. Follow-up post-hoc tests (which we won’t be covering) are then used to compare specific pairs of groups, while still controlling the overall false-alarm rate across all those follow-up comparisons — same multiple-comparisons logic as above, just applied one level down.
ANOVA carries the same core assumptions as the t-test (normality within groups, roughly equal variances across groups, independence) — which should feel natural, since a two-group ANOVA and an independent t-test are actually mathematically equivalent (in that special case, \(F = t^2\)).

Kruskal-Wallis test
The natural extension of the Mann-Whitney U idea to three-or-more groups, and the nonparametric counterpart to one-way ANOVA: pool all observations across every group, rank them, and ask whether the average rank differs suspiciously across groups — without requiring normality or equal variances. Use it exactly when you’d want ANOVA but its assumptions are badly violated.

title: lectures-lecture5
text:
Comparing categorical outcomes
So far, every test has assumed a continuous (or at least ordered) outcome. Now suppose your outcome is a category with no natural numeric scale — recovered/not recovered, voted yes/no/abstain, defective/not defective.

Chi-square test (two flavors)
The chi-square test is really a single unifying idea used to answer two different-sounding questions.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: The intuition: compare what you counted to what you expected
text:
The intuition: compare what you counted to what you expected
In both flavors, the logic is the same: compute how many observations you’d expect to see in each category if \(H_0\) were exactly true, then compare that to what you actually counted. Cells where the observed count is way off from the expected count contribute a lot of “surprise”; cells that land close to expectations contribute little. Add up the surprise, cell by cell, and you get the chi-square statistic:
\[\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(\text{observed} - \text{expected})^2}{\text{expected}}\]
Squaring the gaps means both “way more than expected” and “way less than expected” count as equally surprising, and dividing by the expected count keeps a given raw gap from mattering more just because that cell happened to have a bigger expected count to begin with.
Type 1 — goodness-of-fit: does a single categorical variable follow some hypothesized distribution? (E.g., “are these dice fair?” — expecting roughly 1/6 of rolls in each face.)
Type 2 — test of independence (or association): are two categorical variables related, or independent of one another? (E.g., “is smoking status associated with disease outcome?”) Here, the “expected counts” are calculated as if the two variables had no relationship at all (using each variable’s own marginal totals), and the test asks whether the actual cross-tabulated counts deviate from that no-relationship baseline.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: When the chi-square test breaks down
text:
When the chi-square test breaks down
The chi-square statistic’s connection to a clean reference (chi-square) distribution is itself only an approximation, and that approximation gets shaky when expected cell counts are small — a common rule of thumb is that it becomes unreliable if any expected count drops below about 5. This is precisely the gap that Fisher’s exact test fills.

Fisher’s exact test
Setting: Comparing two categorical variables (most commonly summarized in a 2×2 table), especially with a small sample size or sparse cells — exactly the situation where the chi-square approximation gets shaky.

title: lectures-lecture5
section: The intuition: count every possible table, exactly
text:
The intuition: count every possible table, exactly
Rather than relying on a large-sample approximation, Fisher’s exact test does something wonderfully literal: holding the row and column totals fixed at what you actually observed, it enumerates every single possible 2×2 table consistent with those totals, computes the exact probability of each one occurring by chance alone (using combinatorics — literally counting arrangements, the way you’d count hands of cards), and then adds up the probabilities of your observed table and every table at least as extreme.
This is the same “counting arrangements” logic behind the classic motivating story for the test — the “Lady Tasting Tea” experiment, where Ronald Fisher tested whether a woman could really distinguish, by taste, whether milk or tea was poured into the cup first, by working out the exact probability of her getting her observed number of correct guesses purely by chance.
Because it computes an exact probability rather than leaning on a large-sample approximation, Fisher’s exact test remains valid even with tiny samples or sparse tables — the cost is that it’s more computationally intensive (historically a real constraint, though a non-issue for modern software) and, with very small samples, can be somewhat conservative (less powerful than you might hope, since only a limited number of “at least as extreme” tables are even possible to compare against).

title: lectures-lecture5
section: How this connects to Hypothesis Testing
text:
How this connects to Hypothesis Testing
It’s worth being explicit that nothing new is philosophically happening here — we’re just plugging different data structures into the same engine:

Every test above still produces a p-value, interpreted exactly as in Lecture 1: “how surprising would this data be if \(H_0\) (no group difference / no association) were true?”
Every test above has a matching effect size, and reporting it is just as important here as it was in Lecture 2: Cohen’s \(d\) for t-tests, \(\eta^2\) (eta-squared) for ANOVA, and Cramér’s V or an odds ratio for chi-square/Fisher’s tables. A “highly significant” chi-square result from a huge sample can still reflect a trivially small association — the same lesson from Lecture 2, just wearing a categorical-data costume.
Power analysis still applies to every test here — before running a study, you’d still ask “given my expected effect size and my planned sample size, is my chosen test even likely to detect a real difference if one exists?” The four-dial power picture from Lecture 2 (sample size, effect size, \(\alpha\), noise) governs a chi-square test or an ANOVA exactly as much as it governs a simple two-sample t-test.
The parametric/nonparametric split you saw today (t-test vs. Mann-Whitney, ANOVA vs. Kruskal-Wallis) is really a Fisher-information trade-off: parametric tests squeeze out more information — and thus more power — if their assumptions hold, because they use the full numeric structure of the data rather than just its ranks. Nonparametric tests deliberately throw away some of that structure (keeping only the ranks) in exchange for working correctly under a much wider range of real-world conditions.

title: lectures-lecture5
text:
Summary

The single biggest fork in choosing a group-comparison test is continuous vs. categorical outcome — that decision alone points you toward the t-test/ANOVA family or the chi-square/Fisher’s family.
Within the continuous-outcome family, further ask how many groups, paired or independent, and are parametric assumptions reasonable — these three answers select among t-test, paired t-test, ANOVA, Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and Kruskal-Wallis.
Within the categorical-outcome family, ask one variable against a hypothesized shape, or association between two variables — and if the latter, whether your expected cell counts are large enough to trust the chi-square approximation, or small enough that you need Fisher’s exact test instead.
All of these are hypothesis tests in the Lecture 1 sense, all deserve an accompanying effect size as in Lecture 2, and all are subject to the same power-analysis logic — the “zoo” of named tests is really one underlying idea, repeatedly adapted to different data shapes.
